content: 1. The intervention being evaluated is spinal manipulative therapy (SMT) for the non-surgical management of chronic primary low back pain in adults, including older adults aged 60 years and above. The analysis considers the benefits and harms of SMT compared to usual care, sham interventions, or no intervention. 2. Confidence intervals (CI), mean differences (MD), and standardized mean differences (SMD) are used to assess the outcomes. The quality of evidence is graded using the GRADE approach, with downgrades applied for specific biases or limitations in the studies. 3. The evidence was downgraded due to performance bias, as none of the trials included patient blinding. However, no downgrades were applied for other risk of bias domains because the majority of the evidence weight came from trials with a low risk of bias. 4. Statistical heterogeneity was observed (I² = 68%), which could not be explained by subgroup analysis. The treatment effects and corresponding 95% confidence intervals varied in direction, leading to a downgrade in the quality of evidence. 5. Evidence was downgraded because the data were derived exclusively from single-center trials, limiting generalizability to different settings or countries. 6. The upper 95% confidence interval crossed the threshold of potential clinical relevance, while the lower boundary was close to no effect. This led to a downgrade in the evidence quality. 7. The evidence was downgraded due to an insufficient number of participants (<2000) contributing data to the outcome. 8. High risk of performance bias (lack of patient blinding), attrition bias, and selective reporting bias were present, leading to a downgrade in the evidence quality. 9. No downgrades were applied when the I² statistic was less than 50%, and there was sufficient overlap of the 95% confidence intervals. 10. Evidence was downgraded due to the small number of participants recruited in the studies. 11. Evidence was downgraded when data were derived from a single small trial. 12. Massage therapy was defined as the manual manipulation of soft tissues to enhance health and well-being. It is practiced globally in over 80 different forms, many of which have been developed in the last 30 years. Massage can be applied to specific body parts, such as the lumbar region, or to the entire body. 13. The evidence review for massage therapy included any form of soft tissue manipulation using hands or mechanical devices, as well as traditional, complementary, and integrative (TCI) medicine massage techniques. 14. The critical outcomes assessed for chronic primary low back pain included pain, back-specific function/disability, general function/disability, health-related quality of life, psychosocial function, social participation, adverse events, changes in medication use, and falls. 15. No evidence synthesis was commissioned for all adults or older adults regarding values, preferences, equity, human rights, acceptability, or feasibility. Judgments were based on the experience of the Guideline Development Group (GDG) members. 16. Evidence for massage therapy was downgraded due to selection bias (unclear treatment allocation), performance bias (unclear co-interventions and compliance), and selective outcome reporting bias. 17. Some studies were downgraded because they included specific populations, such as only women over 65 years of age, or used different forms of massage (e.g., reflexology instead of spinal massage). 18. Evidence was downgraded when the number of participants was very small (approximately 200 or fewer) or when the 95% confidence intervals were relatively broad. 19. Traction therapy was defined as the application of a distraction force to the spine's long axis, achieved using body weight, external weights, or pulleys. It can be intermittent or continuous and applied for varying durations. 20. The critical outcomes for traction therapy were the same as those for massage therapy, including pain, function/disability, quality of life, psychosocial function, social participation, adverse events, medication use, and falls. 21. Evidence for traction therapy was downgraded due to high risk of bias, including unclear treatment allocation, lack of blinding, and insufficient participant numbers. 22. The evidence synthesis for traction therapy was limited, with judgments based on the experience of GDG members rather than comprehensive evidence synthesis.
